▰ The story of the terminal begins long before graphical interfaces existed. In the 1960s, teletypewriters like the
  Teletype Model 33 served as the primary interface between humans and expensive mainframe computers. These devices used
  noisy electromechanical print heads and paper roll feeders — far from silent or sleek, but revolutionary in their
  ability to let users interact with computing machines remotely. By the late 1960s, the VT100 emerged from DEC and
  became an enduring standard, introducing escape codes and a character grid that shaped how generations of programmers
  thought about screen-based interaction. The term "terminal" originally described dedicated hardware boxes connected to
  mainframes via serial cables; users typed commands and received text output in real time.

  With the advent of personal computing in the 1970s and 1980s, terminals evolved into software emulators running on
  individual machines. Unix systems popularized the terminal emulator as a window within a windowing system, while the
  rise of Linux gave millions their first command-line experience through xterm and similar programs. The terminal
  endured even as mouse-driven desktop environments took over, because its text-based paradigm remained unmatched for
  scripting, remote server administration, and direct machine communication. Modern terminals carry this legacy forward,
  supporting rich color palettes, ligatures, and GPU-accelerated rendering while still operating on decades-old
  foundations. Projects like tmux, zsh plugins, and Neovim prove that developers still find profound value in that
  original text-in, text-out loop — a workflow refined over sixty years, from clanking teletypes to the sleek terminal
  windows we open every day.

  teletype keys click down screens glow in darkened rooms code flows, text remains
